{{Short description|Optical system example}}[[File:Sine condition.svg|thumb|right|400px|Entrance and exit rays through an imaging system (grey box).]]In [[optics]], the '''Herschel's condition''' is a condition for an [[optical system]] to produce sharp images for objects over an extended axial range, i.e. for objects displaced along the optical axis. It was formulated by [[John Herschel]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Herschel | first=John Frederick William | year=1821 | title=XVII. On the aberrations of compound lenses and object-glasses | journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society | volume=111 | pages=222–267 | doi=10.1098/rstl.1821.0018 }}</ref>

==Mathematical formulation==
The Herschel's condition in mathematical form is
<math display="block">\frac{1-\cos \alpha_\mathrm{o}}{1-\cos \alpha_\mathrm{i}} = \frac{1-\cos \beta_\mathrm{o}}{1-\cos \beta_\mathrm{i}} = \frac{n_i^2}{n_o^2}|M_T|^2</math>
where <math>\alpha_o,\beta_o</math> are the object side ray angles, <math>\alpha_i,\beta_i</math> are the image side ray angle. <math>n_o,n_i</math> are the object and image side [[refractive index]], and <math>M_T</math> is the transverse magnification. This condition can be derived by the [[Fermat's principle]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Braat |first=Joseph J. M. |title=Fifth International Topical Meeting on Education and Training in Optics |date=1997-12-08 |chapter=Abbe sine condition and related imaging conditions in geometrical optics |volume=3190 |chapter-url=http://proceedings.spiedigitallibrary.org/proceeding.aspx?doi=10.1117/12.294417 |pages=59 |doi=10.1117/12.294417}}</ref>

This condition can also be expressed as<ref name=Bass2009>{{cite book | last1=Bass | first1=Michael | last2=DeCusatis | first2=Casimer M. | last3=Enoch | first3=Jay M. | last4=Lakshminarayanan | first4=Vasudevan | last5=Li | first5=Guifang | last6=MacDonald | first6=Carolyn | last7=Mahajan | first7=Virendra N. | last8=Van Stryland | first8=Eric | title=Handbook of Optics, Third Edition, Volume I: Geometrical and Physical Optics, Polarized Light, Components and Instruments | date=22 September 2009 | edition=3rd | publisher=McGraw Hill | location=New York | language=English | isbn=978-0071498890 }}</ref>{{rp|§1.9}}<ref>{{cite book | last1=Gross | first1=Herbert | last2=Zügge | first2=Hannfried | last3=Peschka | first3=Martin | last4=Blechinger | first4=Fritz | title=Handbook of Optical Systems, Volume 3: Aberration Theory and Correction of Optical Systems | publisher=Wiley-VCH | date=9 April 2007 | edition=1st | isbn=978-3527403790 | doi=10.1002/9783527699254 }}</ref>{{rp|§29.8}}
<math display="block">M_L = \frac{n_o\sin^2 (\alpha_\mathrm{o}/2)}{n_i\sin^2 (\alpha_\mathrm{i}/2)}=\frac{n_o(1-\cos \alpha_\mathrm{o})}{n_i(1-\cos \alpha_\mathrm{i})} \text{ and } M_T = \frac{n_o\sin (\alpha_\mathrm{o}/2)}{n_i\sin (\alpha_\mathrm{i}/2)} 
</math>
where <math>M_L = \frac{n_i}{n_o}M_T^2 </math> is the longitudinal magnification.

This condition is in general conflict with the [[Abbe sine condition]], which is the condition for aberration free imaging for objects displaced off-axis. They can be simultaneously satisfied only when the system has magnification equal to the ratio of refractive index <math>|M_T|=n_o/n_i</math>.<ref name="Bass2009" />{{rp|§1.9}}
